expect: 2 marks per difference (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The kalam argument (al-Ghazali) focuses specifically on the beginning of the universe — 'everything that begins to exist has a cause' — whereas Aquinas's Third Way focuses on contingency — things might not exist, requiring a necessary being (2); the kalam originates in Islamic rational theology (ilm al-kalam), developed by al-Ghazali in the 11th century, whereas Aquinas's ways originate in Catholic scholastic theology and draw on Aristotelian philosophy (2).
value: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: everything that begins to exist has a cause, and Muslims hold that the universe began to exist, so it must have a cause outside itself — al-Ghazali identifies that cause as Allah (2); the first cause must be timeless, uncaused and immensely powerful, which matches the Muslim understanding of Allah as the eternal creator of everything (2).

value: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Case for the statement: the scale of suffering — famine, disease, the death of children — looks out of proportion to any purpose, and atheists and Humanists argue that a compassionate God would prevent it. Muslim case: Surah 1 names Allah as Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim; Surah 2:155-157 teaches that life is a test (dunya as imtihaan); Surah 2:153 promises that Allah is with the patient; Surah 2:177 makes charity a practical response. Evaluate whether the test framework answers the scale of the suffering. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, sources named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided.
